lesson.grammar_point: future forms: will vs going to vs present continuous for arrangements

listenings.text: I organize partnership meetings every week, and I always start with the agenda. I write it three days before the meeting, and I circulate it the same day. First, I write the objective in one sentence. What do we want at the end of this call? Then I choose three agenda items, sometimes four, never more. Each item has a time slot and a name. For example, fifteen minutes, Daniel presents the new program. At the start of the meeting, I ask one person to take the minutes. And if something important comes up during the call, I say: good point, we are going to put it on the next agenda.

Last year I had a meeting with a partner from Mexico, and we had no agenda. We started with a small subject, the date of an event, and we talked about it for about forty minutes. Everybody had an opinion. Then somebody looked at the clock, and we had only five minutes left. The important subject, the budget, never happened. We had to reschedule, and the partner was not happy. Now I have a simple rule. I am going to send an agenda before every meeting, with a time slot for each item. And if a discussion takes too long, I will stop it and prioritize.

the written record of what people said and decided in a meeting
to send a document to all the people in a group

paras: Many people think that a meeting starts when the call starts. Good organizers disagree. For them, a meeting starts two or three days before, with one short page: the agenda. The agenda says what the objective of the meeting is, which subjects the attendees are going to discuss, and how much time each subject has.

The most useful agendas are short. Three or four agenda items are usually enough for one hour. Each item has a time slot and the name of the person who is going to present it. When an organizer circulates the agenda early, the attendees can prepare, and people who speak a second language can check the words they need. That is a big difference in an international meeting.

An agenda also helps the person who runs the meeting. When a discussion is taking too long, she can look at the page and say: we have five minutes left for this item. And at the end, the person who takes the minutes can follow the same page. If a meeting has no agenda, it usually has no minutes either, and a week later nobody remembers what the group decided.
